title: A Study on Expectation Adjustment to Minimize Side Effects in Psychotherapy
summary:
Like medical treatment, psychotherapeutic treatment requires the patient to be informed and to give their consent before it begins. However, there are currently no clear, scientifically proven rules on exactly how this information should be provided in psychotherapy. In practice, the risks of psychotherapy are often not explained consistently or sufficiently. As a result, patients may have false or overly negative expectations of the treatment. However, studies show that positive expectations can improve the success of therapy.
This study therefore investigates whether an optimized information strategy for psychotherapy is effective. An online study is being conducted for this purpose. Participants watch a short video of a (simulated) initial consultation with a therapist who provides information about psychotherapy and possible side effects. Participants then complete questionnaires about their expectations of therapy and other important factors—in particular, how stressful they find the side effects mentioned.
conditions: For the study, test subjects recruited online, without previous experience of psychotherapy are to be examined

interventions.name: Control group: Video (2 minutes) displaying conventional, neutral information about side effects in psychotherapy  (total duration: approx. 20 min)
Intervention group: Expectation-optimized information (2 Minutes) about side effects in psychotherapy  (total duration: approx. 20 min)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Interest in participating
Exclusion criteria:
Previous experience with psychotherapy, hearing or visual impairments that may interfere with viewing audiovisual sequences
